title: The thunder glorifies
hookLine: the thunder glorifies His praise, and the angels too, in awe (13:13)

lines: A FLASH; THE ROOM GOES WHITE.
cards: A summer storm at night. The flash first, so bright the room goes white. Then you start counting, the way kids do: one, two, three.
Then the sound, rolling across the roof, rattling the windows, so deep you feel it in your chest. Grown adults still flinch. Surah thirteen of the Qur'an is named for that sound.
Ar-Ra'd: the thunder. And it hears something in that sound besides noise.

teach.b: Verse twelve, in paraphrase: it is He who shows you the lightning, bringing fear and hope, and raises the heavy clouds. Fear of the strike, hope of the rain; for people in a dry land, both are real.
Then verse thirteen, in Pickthall's translation: "The thunder hymneth His praise and (so do) the angels for awe of Him." The thunder isn't just a noise here. It's praising.
The Qur'an says this in more than one place: another surah says there is nothing that doesn't glorify God with praise, but you don't understand their praise.
Elsewhere it names the birds and the mountains among those that praise. Scholars read it in different ways. Some take it as real praise, in a language people can't follow.

Some take it as the praise of a creature simply being what it was made to be. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi describes thunder as an angel charged with the clouds, and scholars discuss the strength of that report.

Imam Malik records that 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, a companion, would stop talking when he heard thunder, and say: glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels, in awe of Him.
Some Muslims still say his words during a storm. A frightening sound, heard as praise, and a conversation paused out of respect, the way talk stops when someone nearby starts to pray.

how: When they hear thunder, some Muslims pause and repeat the words reported from 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr in Malik's Muwatta: glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels in awe of Him.

o: the lightning flash that comes before a storm
the thunder, the name of Surah thirteen
the rain that answers a long dry season

s: Surah 13 is named for the thunder
ar-Ra'd means the thunder; verse 13 says it hymns God's praise.
the Qur'an says only people and angels glorify God
another surah says there's nothing that doesn't glorify Him, though we don't understand their praise.
the lightning in 13:12 brings only fear
fear and hope: fear of the strike, hope of the rain.

games.q: you're 'Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr, mid-conversation, and thunder rolls overhead. what do you do?
o: stop talking, and glorify the One the thunder glorifies.
go inside and shut the windows.
games.why: he stopped talking and said: glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels in awe of Him.

practice: Listen to whatever sound is around you: rain or wind if you have it, or traffic, a fan, the hum of a fridge. Don't name it; just listen, the way you'd listen to someone praying in another room.
If you pray, you can say Ibn az-Zubayr's words, or simply subhanallah, glory be to God.
